Key Stats for AT&T Stock

Current Price: $23.50

Target Price (Mid): ~$39

Street Target: ~$29

Potential Total Return: ~65%

Annualized IRR: ~13% / year

What Happened?

Bernstein downgraded AT&T (T) to Market Perform late on Oct. 12, cutting its target to $24 from $25 over SpaceX's push into broadband and wireless. The stock closed at $23.50 on Oct. 15.

AT&T reports Q3 results before the open on Oct. 21. It is likely the last report for CFO Pascal Desroches, who retires on Dec. 31. At a Bank of America conference on Sept. 10, he laid out where growth is supposed to come from, and the investor relations materials will show whether it is arriving.

The Lumen Gap Is Still AT&T's to Close

Desroches' clearest growth lever was the Lumen footprint. AT&T bought about 4.5 million consumer locations that were "about 25% penetrated as compared to 40%" in its own territory, and he expects "gradual improvements over the next several quarters."

On Oct. 6, AT&T agreed to fold Forged Fiber 37, the unit holding the Lumen network, and Gigapower into a wholesale fiber joint venture with GIP and CPP Investments. Key terms:

Ownership: AT&T will hold 50%, and the deal should close in the first half of 2027.

Customers: The Lumen customer relationships stay with AT&T's home internet business. At closing, the venture is expected to serve more than 1 million AT&T fiber subscribers.

Accounting: AT&T will continue reporting Forged Fiber 37 as held for sale until closing. Afterward, it will book its share of the venture's earnings rather than consolidating it.

Proceeds: The cash AT&T receives at closing will help it reach net debt of about 2.5 times adjusted EBITDA within roughly three years.

Convergence, meaning customers who buy both home internet and wireless from AT&T, is the second gauge:

Fixed wireless: Desroches said that base is already above 50%.

All internet customers: BofA analyst Michael Funk put the share also taking AT&T postpaid wireless at 42.5% after Q2, and 45% outside the Lumen footprint.

Target: Jenifer Robertson, who leads AT&T's consumer business, restated the 50% goal.

AT&T Net Debt / EBITDA (TIKR)
What Bernstein Flagged and What Q3 Has to Clear

The downgrade followed Oct. 9, when AT&T, Verizon (VZ) and T-Mobile (TMUS) fell together after SpaceX (SPCX) agreed to buy Grain Management's 800 MHz spectrum. That deal still needs FCC approval. The selloff also landed in a week when the 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.36%, a 24-year high.

Bernstein also cited recent pricing moves by incumbents and expected fourth-quarter seasonality. AT&T was the last of five big wireless and cable stocks it rated Outperform, though it said Starlink is not a direct threat to AT&T's fiber. Its $24 target sits below the Street mean of around $29.

AT&T (NYSE:T) agreed to sell its Mexican wireless operations to Grupo Televisa and Fintech Holdings in a newly announced deal.

The transaction covers AT&T's consumer and enterprise mobile business in Mexico, shifting those subscribers to the two buyers.

Management framed the exit from Mexico as a way to direct more resources toward U.S. fiber and 5G network buildout.

The decision to sell AT&T's Mexican wireless unit is important. Investors also need to weigh other business pressures and capital choices. We have also spotted 4 warning signs (1 major) worth knowing about at AT&T.

Consider broadening your watchlist by reviewing other telecom and infrastructure stocks with exposure to wired and wireless networks through 41 power grid technology and infrastructure stocks.

NYSE:T Earnings & Revenue Growth as at Oct 2026

AT&T is a large US telecom provider with a market value of about $157.9b. This Mexico exit sits alongside its broader role supplying mobile and technology services across its core domestic network footprint.

4 things going right for AT&T that this headline doesn't cover.

AT&T's Mexico exit puts its fiber‑first bet under a brighter spotlight

AT&T's Narrative is built around a simple trade off. Pour money and management focus into U.S. fiber and 5G, then shrink older networks and lower returning ventures enough that recurring service revenue and cost savings carry the load.

"The key requirement is that AT&T executes on large scale fiber build out, copper retirement, and cost take out while managing device subsidies..."

See how the full story points towards a $29.05 fair value for AT&T.

The Mexico sale leans into the bullish version of that story. Management is choosing to simplify the business model and recycle capital from a non core wireless market into U.S. fiber build, where the Narrative already highlights convergence, copper retirement and recurring service revenue as the main engine. For holders who back that thesis, this looks like alignment rather than a change in direction.

The bear side does not disappear, though. Leaving Mexico trims diversification at a time when analysts already flag high debt, heavy device promotions and earnings that are forecast to decline on current estimates. If Verizon or T Mobile can scale cross border or adjacent services more effectively, AT&T's tighter geographic focus could be read as concentration risk rather than discipline.

In the end, this same transaction can either confirm a cleaner fiber led AT&T story or underline execution and concentration risks, depending on which Narrative you already believe.

The decline has left a company still growing its sales priced below its own historical baseline: the shares currently trade at 16.2 times earnings, against an average of 21.9 across its last twelve fiscal quarter-ends. So how much of that lost ground could T-Mobile win back over the next three years?

What T-Mobile Shares Would Be Worth On These Assumptions

Under these assumptions, T-Mobile shares would be worth about $226.72 in three years, compared with $157.03 at the October 15, 2026 close. That represents a 44.4% gain before dividends, and it would return the shares to about their highest close of the past year, reached on October 20, 2025.

Most of the gain, 64.6%, would come from T-Mobile selling more. A higher P/E accounts for most of the remainder. The company saw revenue grow in fiscal Q2 2026 on growth in its postpaid business, and management said postpaid service revenue rose 13% that quarter. The higher P/E is a Trefis assumption rather than a finding: the scenario moves today's multiple 40% of the way back toward its own past, capping that historical baseline at 1.3 times today's P/E.

T-Mobile Has To Keep Adding Accounts And Charging More

To achieve that gain, T-Mobile has to keep adding customers and getting more from each one. So far, its sales growth has accelerated. Revenue grew 0.7% in the twelve months to June 2024 and 6.3% in the twelve months to June 2025. Over the twelve months to June 2026, revenue grew 9.7%, a pace faster than the scenario assumes for the next three years.

T-Mobile added 277,000 postpaid accounts in fiscal Q2 2026. Management's fiscal 2026 guidance, issued in a July 23 release, includes postpaid net account additions of 950,000 to 1,050,000. That estimate sits alongside targets for profit, cash flow and capital spending. Management also expects revenue per postpaid account to grow 2.5% to 3% in fiscal 2026.

In July, management said it expected about 250,000 net postpaid account additions in fiscal Q3 2026, the quarter that ended in September. It also noted that its rate plan modernization is expected to lift account churn for a while.
